extracted.intended_audience: federal judges and litigators handling Voting Rights Act and election-law litigation
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and procedural rules for evaluating Section 5 Voting Rights Act claims, related Fifteenth Amendment/§1971/§1973 claims, and associated federal jurisdiction/pleading issues in federal district and appellate litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-judge court requirement for Section 5 actions
rubrics_metrics.description: 42 U.S.C. §1973(c) requires that 'any action under this section should be heard and determined by a court of three judges in accordance with the provisions of section 2284 of Title 28.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Private parties may bring a Section 5 coverage action in any U.S. District Court over which three judges shall preside to determine the coverage issue; coverage questions generally must be determined by a three-judge court (Allen v. State Board of Elections).

rubrics_metrics.name: Single judge's authority to determine need for three-judge court and to dismiss insubstantial Section 5 claims
rubrics_metrics.description: The single judge district court may make the determination regarding whether there is a Section 5 coverage question presented by the pleadings which would require a three-judge court and may also make the decision to dismiss a meritless claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 28 U.S.C. §2284(b)(3) and precedent (U.S. v. Saint Landry Parish School Board, Backus v. Spears, Webber v. White) allow a single judge to determine if a three-judge court is required; a three-judge court is not required if the claim is wholly insubstantial or completely without merit, and the single judge may dismiss such claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single judge may enter dismissal orders under Rule 12(b)(6) even when Section 5 involved
rubrics_metrics.description: A dismissal for failure to state a claim under Rule 12(b)(6) of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure is not a judgment on the merits and is clearly an 'order permitted by the rules of civil procedure'. Therefore, such an order may be entered by a single judge even though the provisions of Section 5 are involved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authority to dismiss for failure to state a cause of action emanates from 28 U.S.C. §2284(3): 'A single judge may conduct all proceedings except the trial, and enter all orders permitted by the rules of civil procedure except as provided in this subsection.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of inquiry in private Section 5 actions
rubrics_metrics.description: An action brought by a private litigant under Section 5, 42 U.S.C. §1973(c), is of a very limited nature. The court’s scope of inquiry is limited to whether or not the voting change is covered by Section 5 and if the change is covered, whether the Section 5 requirements were satisfied by submission to the Justice Department for clearance or by an action for declaratory judgment in the District Court of the District of Columbia.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the District Court determines that a voting change is within the purview of Section 5, it may issue an injunction against enforcement until the State has properly submitted the change; otherwise relief under §5 is unavailable to private parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of Justice Department preclearance/approval under Section 5
rubrics_metrics.description: Once the State has successfully complied with the Section 5 submission and approval requirements, there is no further action or remedy provided for by Section 5.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If approval is obtained, the matter will be at an end (citing Allen v. State Board of Elections; Berry v. Doles). Letters from the Attorney General interposing no objections constitute evidence that the change was precleared and render §5 claims without merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: What constitutes a 'change' subject to Section 5 coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: The approval requirements of Section 5 apply only when 'a state or political subdivision shall enact or seek to administer' a change in voting procedures. Actions that are deviations from a state's required procedures or isolated official misconduct do not necessarily constitute a change the state 'enacts or seeks to administer.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deviations by state officials (election fraud or irregularities) are not automatically changes subject to §5; courts consider the language of §5, the nature of approval provisions, and relevant cases (United States v. Saint Landry Parish School Board).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleading requirements for statutory claims (general)
rubrics_metrics.description: Merely alleging a violation of a statute is insufficient; all elements encompassing the offense must be adequately pled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pleadings that do nothing more than track the statutes on which they attempt to base a claim are not well pled. Such language constitutes unsupported legal conclusions cast in the form of factual allegations; pleadings that rely on such language fail to state a cause of action (Webber v. White).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleading requirements for Fifteenth Amendment and §2/§1971 claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims under the Fifteenth Amendment and related statutory provisions must allege that plaintiffs were actually denied the right to register or to vote based on race, color, or previous condition of servitude and must allege discriminatory intent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absent invidious purpose there can be no Fifteenth Amendment claim (Gomillion v. Lightfoot; Arlington Heights; Washington v. Davis). Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act is parallel to the Fifteenth Amendment and §1971 involves the same type of racial discrimination; mere recitation of minority status or statutory language is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insubstantial claim standard
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim is insubstantial if prior Supreme Court decisions 'inescapably render the claim frivolous.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a claim is wholly insubstantial or completely without merit, a single judge need not convene a three-judge court and may dismiss the claim (citing Goosby v. Osser, Saint Landry, Backus).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pendent (supplemental) jurisdiction standards
rubrics_metrics.description: If the pleadings disclose a substantial federal claim, there is power to hear pendent claims that 'derive from a common nucleus of operative fact' and that the plaintiff would ordinarily be expected to try in one judicial proceeding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the federal claim is too insubstantial to be the basis for federal-question jurisdiction, there can be no pendent jurisdiction of other claims (United Mine Workers v. Gibbs; Junker v. Crory). Even where power exists, exercising pendent jurisdiction is discretionary, considering judicial economy, convenience and fairness.

rubrics_metrics.name: 28 U.S.C. §2283 anti-injunction statute constraint
rubrics_metrics.description: 28 U.S.C. §2283 prohibits a court of the United States from enjoining proceedings in a State court except where necessary in aid of its jurisdiction or to protect or effectuate its judgments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal courts lack authority under §2283 to enjoin ongoing state proceedings unless a statutory exception applies; this limits federal relief for state-law election claims when state litigation is pending.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precedent regarding Article 717m-1 bond statute constitutionality
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 717m-1 (Vernon’s) has been held constitutional by Texas courts and the Supreme Court’s dismissal of a related appeal indicated a want of a substantial federal question.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases cited (Buckholts ISD v. Glasser; Rio Grande Valley Sugar Growers; Asmussen) support that bond requirements do not present a substantial federal question and that the bond is required only if the intervenor is unable to convince the trial court of invalidity; bond requirement is not a denial of due process and serves legislative purpose to stop frivolous suits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arguments raised for the first time on appeal are improper
rubrics_metrics.description: An argument improperly raised for the first time on appeal and not supported by the record will not be entertained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Matter of Novack (639 F.2d 1274) cited: petitioners’ new argument that there was an incomplete submission rendering clearance ineffective was neither raised nor supported by the record and is impermissible on appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of administrative letters as conclusive evidence of preclearance
rubrics_metrics.description: Letters from the Attorney General indicating 'The Attorney General does not interpose any objections to the changes in question' establish that the elections and procedures were submitted and interposed no objections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such letters 'clearly establish' preclearance and support dismissal of §5 claims as without merit where the record contains them (example: DOJ letters dated Feb 7 and Mar 3, 1986).
